comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
## /rebar-debug — Phase 1 RCA (root cause CONFIRMED at runtime)

### Proven root cause

The materiality test is a **hash-equality check over the whole `file_impact` list**, so it is
structurally incapable of telling an ADDITION from a REMOVAL or a rewrite.

`llm/plan_review/material_diff.py:110` `material_basis()` builds the basis with
`"file_impact": ctx.state.get("file_impact") or []`, and `_hash_component()` (:155) hashes that
list wholesale. Any mutation changes the digest; the digest is the only signal downstream
(`llm/plan_review/attest.py:582` emits `"verdict": "stale-material"`).

The two gates therefore demand mutually exclusive things:

- **Gate 1** — `_commands/close_precheck.py:302-310` computes `undeclared_paths(...)` and refuses
  the close, instructing: *"Declare them with `rebar set-file-impact <ticket> ...` **and retry**"*.
- **Gate 2** — following that instruction changes the `file_impact` hash, so the retry is refused
  as `stale-material`.

### Runtime proof (executed, not read)

Driving the real functions from the installed package:

```
signed  hash: c3ec16dd33b8418d
widened hash: c251cc50b5cd4233   CHANGED? True     <- purely ADDITIVE (+1 generated path)
removed hash: 9708be1d47b72913   CHANGED? True     <- REMOVAL
```

An additive widening and a removal are **equally "different"**. There is no residue in the
comparison from which additivity could be recovered — confirming the cause is the hash-wholesale
design, not a missing branch somewhere downstream.

The same run confirms the fix pattern already exists in this very module:

```
checkbox tick normalized equal? True
```

`normalize_checkbox_state()` (`material_diff.py:66`) exists precisely so ticking an AC checkbox
does not stale an attestation. So "normalize away a change that must not count as material" is an
established, shipped concept here — the fix extends a precedent rather than inventing one.

### Legitimacy: `defect` (not intended behavior)

Cited authority — `_commands/close_precheck.py:307-309`. The gate's own remediation text promises
`"and retry"`. A remediation instruction that the system then rejects is a broken contract on its
face; this is not a matter of the reporter's expectation.

### The constraint any fix must respect

`docs/plan-review-gate.md:1062` states the purpose of `stale-material` verbatim:

> `stale-material` — you attested and then edited the plan — still blocks, **so the gate is not
> bypassable by editing after signing.**

This **rules out** the broadest candidate the ticket floats ("a purely ADDITIVE `file_impact`
correction is a candidate for not staling the attestation"). Blanket-additive would create exactly
the bypass the gate exists to prevent: after signing, an author could add any path — say
`src/rebar/_commands/txn.py` — and close against work no reviewer ever saw. Additive is not
synonymous with harmless.

What is genuinely safe is narrower: the paths in Gate 1's refusal are **computed by the gate from
the commit** (`commit_impact.undeclared_paths`), not chosen by the author. A widening whose
additions are a subset of what the gate itself just demanded introduces no author discretion, so
it cannot be a bypass vector. That distinction — gate-directed vs author-chosen — is the seam the
fix should cut along, and it is strictly narrower than "additive".

### Cross-link to the P1

`close_precheck.py:328` runs `subprocess.run(["git", "-C", ..., "log", "--format=..."])` over the
repository's entire history with **no `timeout=`** — one of the 61 unguarded subprocess sites found
while investigating `unquieting-godsent-mammal` (`b405-d5ec-30b3-4538`), and it sits on the
`transition -> closed` path, which is one of the two operations reported hanging there. Recorded as
an observation; not claimed as that bug's cause, which is still under investigation.

### Not yet done

Defect attribution (`caused_by`) is still outstanding and will be established before any close, per
protocol. Fix design is a security-gate semantics decision and is being put to the operator rather
than chosen unilaterally.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
## RETRACTION — my previous comment's legitimacy verdict was WRONG

I classified this `defect` and proposed exempting "gate-directed" additive `file_impact` changes
from staling. **Both were wrong.** Operator challenge: *justify why these changes CANNOT impact
the plan or introduce plan-review findings.* I cannot, and the code says the opposite.

### `file_impact` is not metadata ABOUT the plan — it DEFINES what the signature covers

`llm/plan_review/read_set.py:4`:

> "…from the ticket's declared ``file_impact`` ∪ the files the review CITED. When a ticket
> declares NO ``file_impact`` that set is empty, and the claim gate degrades to whole-HEAD…"

The attestation's scope is **built from `file_impact`**. Widening 9 -> 15 paths therefore makes an
already-signed attestation assert coverage of **six files no reviewer examined**. That is not a
theoretical bypass — it retroactively broadens what a signature claims.

### It is also a direct input to review, at four sites

- `plan_review/pass1.py:150` `_no_file_impact_context()` -> appended to `context_parts` at :242 —
  it is in the **review prompt**.
- `plan_review/det_lint.py:267` `p9_file_impact_coverage()` — a deterministic criterion scoring
  the declaration; its verdict depends on the path set and on children's scope.
- `plan_review/det_invariants.py:35` `_file_impact_paths()` — invariants computed from the paths.
- `plan_review/det_gate_rules.py`, `registry.py`, `manifest.py` — all consume it.

So a new path can activate criteria that did not previously route, change the blast-radius
assessment, change `next_batch` conflict scheduling, and change the code-drift gate's
invalidation scope. **"Cannot introduce new findings" is false.**

### Corrected legitimacy: `intended-behavior`, NOT `defect`

Cited authority, `docs/plan-review-gate.md:1062`:

> `stale-material` — you attested and then edited the plan — still blocks, **so the gate is not
> bypassable by editing after signing.**

The gate did exactly this. Sequence, read honestly:

1. The plan declared 9 paths and was attested over those 9.
2. The work touched 15.
3. The close gate detected the divergence and refused — **correct**.
4. Widening the declaration to match the work is a **material change to the reviewed plan**.
5. The stale-material gate refused the now-broader plan on an unchanged signature — **also
   correct**.

That is not two gates contradicting each other. It is two gates jointly detecting one real
condition: **the work exceeded its reviewed scope.** The remediation is to re-review, which is
what re-review is for.

### Where my earlier reasoning failed

I cited the gate's own message — "Declare them with `rebar set-file-impact ...` **and retry**"
(`_commands/close_precheck.py:307-309`) — as a broken contract. That over-reads it. "Retry" after
re-attesting the widened plan is a valid and complete path; the message is terse, not
self-contradictory. I turned a terse message into a contract violation to support a conclusion I
had already reached.

### The ticket's own evidence undercuts its premise

The description argues the added paths "could not have been declared at plan time" and that
"neither alters what the plan commits to". But it also states two of them —
`src/rebar/_guides/writing-a-passing-plan.md` and `tests/unit/test_guides.py` — were "absorbed
mid-flight when a Gerrit code review correctly required a sibling story's file to move into this
change". **Absorbing a file from a sibling story is precisely a change to what the plan commits
to**, and `writing-a-passing-plan.md` is a guide governed by its own parity criteria. Only
`criterion-pins.json` (a generated digest) is arguably mechanical, and it did not travel alone.

### Recommended disposition

Close as **not_a_bug**, subject to operator confirmation. The behaviour is the gate working as
designed. Two narrow, genuinely useful residues can be split out if wanted, neither of which
weakens the gate:

1. **Message clarity (docs/UX, small).** `close_precheck.py:307-309` should say that declaring
   new paths is a material plan change and will require re-attestation, instead of implying a bare
   retry suffices. That is what actually misled the filing agent.
2. **Cheap re-attestation, IF it can be made honest.** A re-sign that does not re-run the agentic
   pass is only sound if the reviewer's evidence base is unchanged — and per `read_set.py` it is
   NOT unchanged when paths are added, since the added files were never read. So this is probably
   not available for path additions specifically. Worth a separate ticket only if someone can show
   a class of additions where the read-set provably does not move.

Per `/rebar-debug`'s not-a-bug guard I am **not** implementing a fix. Handing the disposition to
the operator.

comments.body:
## /rebar-debug final report — fix pushed as Gerrit change 1956

### Problem
The close gate's undeclared-paths refusal advertised a remedy ("declare the paths and retry")
whose second half cannot succeed, because declaring them stales the attestation.

### Proven root cause
The materiality test hashes the whole `file_impact` list
(`llm/plan_review/material_diff.py:110` `material_basis`, `:155` `_hash_component`), so any
mutation changes the digest. Runtime-executed, not read:

```
signed  hash: c3ec16dd33b8418d
widened hash: c251cc50b5cd4233   CHANGED? True   <- purely additive
removed hash: 9708be1d47b72913   CHANGED? True   <- removal
```

Additive and destructive edits are equally "different", so nothing downstream could distinguish
them even in principle.

### Scope correction — the gates are NOT the defect
The original framing (and my own first analysis, retracted above) treated this as two gates
contradicting each other and proposed exempting additive widenings. That was wrong:
`llm/plan_review/read_set.py:4` builds the attestation's scope "from the ticket's declared
``file_impact`` ∪ the files the review CITED", so widening it retroactively broadens what an
existing signature claims to cover; and `file_impact` feeds review at four sites
(`pass1.py:242`, `det_lint.py:267`, `det_invariants.py:35`, `det_gate_rules.py`), so a new path
CAN introduce new findings. Both refusals are correct. **The only defect is the message.**

### Defect origin — `cec6-0a0e-38a9-4234`, class `plan_defect`
`git blame -w -C -M -L 302,310` puts every line of the refusal on `746c1ba2e96`
("Add attach-commits verb and impact-vs-diff gate", 2026-08-12, `rebar-ticket: cec6-0a0e-38a9-4234`).

Checked for a carrier: `git log -S'which the recorded file_impact does not declare' --all`
returns **exactly one** commit, and its diffstat is +126 on this file — it CREATED the check and
authored the message. Not a rename, reformat or move.

Applied the date test to rule out an unmet obligation. `stale-material` was introduced by
`2873a91648` on **2026-06-23**, roughly **seven weeks BEFORE** the message was written on
**2026-08-12**. So no later change created this obligation — the gate the remedy collides with
already existed and was already documented when the remedy was authored. That makes this an
**omission at origin**, not a regression and not a missed consumer update.

Sanity check per protocol: could a reviewer of `cec6` plausibly have caught it? Yes — the
interaction was fully present in the tree at review time. That is what makes `plan_defect` the
right class rather than `preexisting`.

The close will carry `--caused-by=cec6-0a0e-38a9-4234 --class=plan_defect` explicitly, so blame
auto-derivation does not add a competing guessed edge beside the proven one.

### Test
`tests/unit/test_close_precheck_message_fb8b.py`, two cases. Observed **RED first** for the right
reason (the fixture asserts it reached the undeclared-paths branch before asserting on wording),
then GREEN. **Mutation check**: re-seeded the defect by deleting the re-attestation clause, the
test returned to RED, restored to GREEN — so it is not a tautology. The second case pins the
existing diagnosis (sha, paths, `set-file-impact`, `--force`) so a future rewrite cannot silently
drop it.

### Fix
`_commands/close_precheck.py` — the refusal now states that the work went beyond the reviewed
plan, that widening `file_impact` is a MATERIAL plan change which invalidates the attestation
(`stale-material`), and that `rebar review-plan` must be re-run before the close can succeed.
**No behavioural change to either gate.**

### Scope & safety
Caller sweep: the message is a leaf string in a `raise CommandError` with no callers depending on
its wording — no test pinned the old text (`grep 'and retry' tests/` found only my own new file's
docstring quoting it). Restores no behaviour and creates none; adds no dependency; weakens no
test. 481 tests pass in the close/gate/file_impact/precheck subset. `make lint`, `make typecheck`
green; complexity ratchet `new=0 increased=0 stale=0`; file at 740/800 LOC.

### Siblings
Precedent, not sibling: `db1c` closed this same class for the bounded-recovery message, and its
docstring names the identical shape — "the advertised remedy for one close gate is a guaranteed
failure of the other, and the message says nothing about that trade." Since two gate messages
have now been found advertising remedies that collide with a sibling gate, a targeted sweep of
the remaining close/claim gate refusals for the same defect is worth doing. **Not swept in this
change** — recorded here as residual rather than silently skipped.

### Replication
The original five-step reproduction now surfaces the re-attestation requirement at step 3, so the
author learns at the first refusal what the second will demand. The loop still exists — correctly
— but is no longer misleading.

### Status
Gerrit **1956**: `LLM-Review +1`, awaiting `Verified`. Attestation re-earned after the scope
rewrite (`rebar review-plan --status` -> `certified`, currency basis `file_impact`). Not closing
until CI is green and the change has merged.

compiled_state.description:
## Problem

The close gate's undeclared-paths refusal tells the author to declare the paths "and retry",
without saying that declaring them is a **material plan change** which invalidates the
plan-review attestation. The bare retry it appears to promise cannot succeed.

`src/rebar/_commands/close_precheck.py:302-310`:

```python
undeclared = commit_impact.undeclared_paths(paths, impact, repo_root=code_root)
if undeclared:
    raise CommandError(
        f"Error: cannot close: commit {sha} changes "
        + ", ".join(undeclared)
        + ", which the recorded file_impact does not declare. Declare them with "
        "`rebar set-file-impact <ticket> ...` and retry "
        '(or override with --force="<reason>").',
```

Following that instruction widens `file_impact`, which changes the material basis hash
(`llm/plan_review/material_diff.py:110-155`), so the next close is refused as `stale-material`
(`llm/plan_review/attest.py:582`). The author reads two refusals as a contradiction, when in fact
both are correct and the missing information is that a **re-review is the required next step**.

## Scope: MESSAGE CLARITY ONLY — the gates are working as designed

This ticket originally proposed exempting additive `file_impact` changes from staling. **That was
investigated and rejected**; see the RETRACTION comment for the full reasoning and citations. In
short:

- `llm/plan_review/read_set.py:4` builds the attestation's scope "from the ticket's declared
  ``file_impact`` ∪ the files the review CITED", so widening `file_impact` retroactively broadens
  what an existing signature claims to cover.
- `file_impact` is a direct review input at four sites (`pass1.py:242` prompt context,
  `det_lint.py:267` `p9_file_impact_coverage`, `det_invariants.py:35`, `det_gate_rules.py`), so a
  new path CAN introduce new findings.
- `docs/plan-review-gate.md:1062` states the gate's purpose: "`stale-material` — you attested and
  then edited the plan — still blocks, **so the gate is not bypassable by editing after signing**."

**No change to gate behaviour is in scope here.** Both refusals must keep firing exactly as they
do. The only defect is that the first message under-describes the remedy.

## Direction

Extend the message so it states three things instead of one: that the work went beyond the
reviewed plan; that declaring the paths is a material change which will invalidate the attestation
(`stale-material`); and that `rebar review-plan <ticket>` must be re-run before the close will
succeed. Keep the existing content — the exact undeclared paths and the `--force` escape hatch.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] The undeclared-paths refusal names re-attestation as a required step: it says that widening
      `file_impact` is a material plan change and that `rebar review-plan` must be re-run before
      the close can succeed.
- [x] The message still names the offending commit sha, the exact undeclared paths, the
      `rebar set-file-impact` remedy, and the `--force="<reason>"` override.
- [x] A test asserts the message names the re-attestation requirement, and would FAIL against the
      current wording — demonstrated by observing it RED before the change.
- [x] No behavioural change to either gate: the undeclared-paths refusal and the `stale-material`
      refusal fire under exactly the conditions they do today, verified by the existing gate tests
      passing unmodified.
- [x] `make lint` and `make typecheck` pass; `python scripts/check_complexity_baseline.py --check`
      reports `new=0 increased=0 stale=0`.

file_impact.reason: Extend the undeclared-paths refusal message to name re-attestation as a required step; no behavioural change.
New test asserting the message names the re-attestation requirement; RED against current wording.

compiled_state.title: Close gate's undeclared-paths message implies a bare retry will work, but declaring paths requires re-attestation
